posts.title: Inside Holocaust memorial in heart of Arab world as founder reveals what changed everything
posts.excerpt: Inside Dubai's Crossroads of Civilizations Museum, founder Ahmed Obaid Al Mansoori reveals how a temporary Holocaust tribute became a permanent gallery.
posts.content:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — In a historic house near Dubai Creek, a small gallery commemorating the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust stands alongside collections exploring Islamic civilization, Emirati heritage and the history of Palestine and the Holy Land.

The Holocaust exhibition at the privately owned Crossroads of Civilizations Museum is among the first permanent displays of its kind in the Arab world. Opened in May 2021, less than a year after the UAE normalized relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords, it has become a symbol of the Emirates' approach to religious coexistence.

During a recent visit to the museum, Fox News Digital saw displays documenting Nazi persecution, including a life-size image of the boy from the famous Warsaw Ghetto photograph, his hands raised in surrender.

The gallery also tells the stories of Muslims who rescued Jews during the Holocaust, including Egyptian physician Mohammed Helmy, who sheltered Jews from Nazi persecution in Berlin.

US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS

But the story behind the exhibition is as personal as the objects it preserves.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, museum founder Ahmed Obaid Al Mansoori, a former member of the UAE's Federal National Council, explained that his passion for collecting historical artifacts began in childhood, when he inherited family manuscripts and objects from his grandparents.

DOMINICAN REPUBLIC JOINS GLOBAL FIGHT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM WITH LANDMARK MOVE

He began collecting systematically in 1989, eventually establishing a private museum in his home in 2006. Dubai authorities later provided a historic building to accommodate his growing collection, which opened to the public in 2014.

The Holocaust gallery came much later.

9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'

Al Mansoori said two experiences inspired him. The first was a visit to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington during the 1990s, where he was deeply moved by the message that the Holocaust was a tragedy with lessons for all humanity.

The second was a conversation with an American Jewish acquaintance who expressed fear about rising antisemitism in the United States. Initially, he dismissed her concerns. But after encountering antisemitic imagery circulating during a period of unrest in the U.S., he reconsidered. "I realized I was wrong," he said.

He turned to Jewish friends and colleagues to organize a Holocaust remembrance event in Dubai in 2021.

CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

"The beauty about this Holocaust gallery was built by Arabs, by Jews, and by Christians," he told Fox News Digital, describing the international team that helped create the exhibition.

What began as a commemorative initiative became something much larger.

At the opening, Al Mansoori said, he was struck by the positive response from visitors, including residents of the UAE and people from elsewhere in the region. He also encountered criticism, but concluded that the gallery should become a permanent part of the museum.

"I thought it was very beautiful, very important. And it must stay," he recalled.

The exhibition formally opened on May 26, 2021, attended by the Israeli and German ambassadors to the UAE, according to The National's coverage at the time.

TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

Yet Al Mansoori's vision extends beyond Holocaust remembrance.

In another section of the museum, historical maps of Palestine appear alongside Jewish manuscripts, photographs and documents illustrating the region's overlapping histories.

"You have the maps from the Israeli perspective. You have the map from the Palestinian perspective," he said, explaining why he deliberately brings different historical narratives into the same space.

He recalled a visit by rabbis in August 2020, when Muslim, Jewish and Christian guests prayed alongside one another at the museum, each according to their own traditions.

For Al Mansoori, the purpose is not to erase religious or political differences, but to make it possible for people to respect one another despite them.

"It's how to learn to be comfortable being yourself next to others. And others must be also comfortable to be next to you," he said.

As war and political tensions continue to divide the Middle East, Al Mansoori believes the museum offers a different way to confront the region's painful history: not by avoiding it, but by allowing visitors to encounter histories and experiences beyond their own.

Source: https://www.foxnews.com/world/inside-holocaust-memorial-heart-arab-world-founder-reveals-changed-everything

posts.title: Duke coach Jon Scheyer says Blue Devils' upset loss to Michigan State felt like an 'out-of-body experience'
posts.excerpt: Jon Scheyer called Duke's 79-73 loss to Michigan State "an out-of-body experience," vowing to fix the Blue Devils' lack of connection on the court.
posts.content:
While many in the college basketball world were surprised to see Duke lose in the fashion it did to Michigan State on Tuesday night, no one was more shocked by the result than Blue Devils head coach Jon Scheyer.

Duke fell to the Spartans, 79-73, but Michigan State controlled the game from the jump. The Spartans scored the opening bucket of the contest 33 seconds after tip, and didn't allow Duke to take the lead once throughout the entire game.

While No. 2 Duke losing on a neutral floor to No. 5 Michigan State by six points won't hurt the Blue Devils' résumé, that doesn't mean Scheyer had the urge to find any positives after his team's loss.

UCONN, KANSAS AND TEXAS OFFER THE BEST COLLEGE BASKETBALL NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP ODDS VALUE

The head coach was sure to give Tom Izzo's Spartans their flowers and respect during his postgame news conference, but made it clear that he was a bit shocked by what he saw from his own team on Tuesday.

"Congrats to Michigan State," Scheyer said during his opening remarks inside the press area. "They 100 percent deserved to win. I thought they outcompeted us. They played more together."

"For me, it was a little bit of an out-of-body experience," Scheyer continued. "Our team, I thought our team, we weren't connected. Just the bottom line, we weren't connected, and we're going to fix it. I promise you that much, and our fans deserve better. That was not a good performance tonight."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The good news for the Blue Devils is that their loss to the Spartans was just their third game of the season, and they have another three-plus months to find the cohesiveness Scheyer was hoping to see against Michigan State.

SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER

The most glaring takeaway from Tuesday's contest was seeing Duke shoot just 33 percent from the field and 70 percent from the free-throw line. The Spartans shot 45 percent from the floor.

Scheyer's squad will be battle-tested multiple times, and soon, with matchups against Top 10 teams Illinois, UConn, and Florida coming between now and December 1.

posts.title: VIDEO: Tinubu Receives Flamingos In Abuja After World Cup Victory
posts.excerpt: The First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, received the victorious players and technical crew on behalf of the President at the Presidential Banquet Hall, Abuja. The post VIDEO: Tinubu Receives Flamingos
posts.content:
President Bola Tinubu has received the Flamingos after winning Africa’s first-ever U-17 FIFA Women’s World Cup in Morocco.

The First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, received the victorious players and technical crew on behalf of the President at the Presidential Banquet Hall, Abuja.

The U-17 team won their first FIFA World Cup title after defeating Japan 2-1 in the final on November 7, with goals from Awawu Bashiru and Oluebube Umejiaku securing the historic victory.

The Flamingos lost their opener 2-1 to Poland, but dominated in the remaining matches, defeating defending champions North Korea, Puerto Rico, and Mexico.

Their first-ever appearance in the final was sealed with a 3-1 victory over Brazil, before taking home the trophy after beating Japan.

Flamingos celebrating their U-17 FIFA Women’s World Cup

The players have received commendations from government officials and football fans around the world.

President Tinubu congratulated the Flamingos for becoming the first African team to win the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup.

Tinubu, in a statement by his spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga, said he received the news upon his return from campaign engagements in Akwa Ibom and Rivers States.

He also described Nigeria’s maiden triumph as a proud moment for the country and a landmark achievement for African women’s football.

The Senate also pledged a ₦100 million reward for the Flamingos.

The pledge followed a motion moved by the Chairman of the Senate Committee on Sports, Senator Abdul Ningi, who congratulated the players on their outstanding performance and commended the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) for its role in the team’s achievement.

The latest feat by a Nigerian sports team came less than two years after the senior women’s football team, Super Falcons, won their 10th Women’s Africa Cup of Nations title in Morocco.

In 2025, the D’Tigress won a historic 2025 FIBA Women’s Afrobasket title.

Source: https://www.channelstv.com/2026/11/11/video-tinubu-receives-flamingos-in-abuja-after-world-cup-victory/

posts.title: ACF crisis deepens as chairman petitions Gov Sani, DSS, police
posts.excerpt: The disagreement within the Arewa Consultative Forum, ACF, has deepened following a petition by the Forum’s Chairman, Maman Mike Osuman, SAN, over the reported break-in at the organisation's national
posts.content:
The disagreement within the Arewa Consultative Forum, ACF, has deepened following a petition by the Forum’s Chairman, Maman Mike Osuman, SAN, over the reported break-in at the organisation's national secretariat in Kaduna.

In a petition dated October 9, 2026, addressed to Governor Uba Sani and copied to the Inspector-General of Police, the Kaduna State Commissioner of Police and the Director of the Department of State Services, DSS, in the state, Osuman raised concerns about developments at the organisation’s headquarters at No. 11A Sokoto Road, Kaduna.

Osuman claimed that some individuals entered the offices, changed locks and removed some items without the consent of the forum’s leadership.

He also claimed that the action was carried out without a search warrant.

Osuman, in the petition, described the development as a matter affecting the institutional integrity of the forum and called on Governor Uba Sani to intervene to prevent further escalation.

“An action of this nature not only affects the sanctity of our corporate headquarters but is also a direct affront to the dignity of the entire Northern Region," the petition said.

The chairman said the national secretariat represented the collective heritage of Northern Nigeria, adding that its protection was important to preserving the dignity and integrity of the organisation.

He urged the governor to ensure that due process prevailed and that the forum was protected from actions capable of undermining its stability.

The latest development has raised concerns over the extent of the disagreement within the organisation, particularly over the control of its national headquarters and the management of its affairs.

It would be recalled that the National Executive Committee, NEC, of the forum had announced the suspension of the Chairman of its Board of Trustees, Alhaji Bashir M. Dalhatu, over alleged breaches of the organisation’s constitution.

The decision followed an emergency NEC meeting held in Kaduna amid tension linked to reported police restriction of access to the ACF headquarters ahead of their gathering in May 2026.

However, the Board of Trustees, BoT, of the forum had dismissed the reported suspension of the chairman, Dalhatu, describing the action as illegal, unconstitutional and an attempt to destabilise the organisation.

The disagreements have exposed divisions among members and stakeholders over who should control the affairs of the northern socio-cultural organisation.

posts.title: Nigeria’s Peace Institute Partners Tech Firm to Scale Peace Education to Millions
posts.excerpt: Yemi Kosoko in Jos In a bold move aimed at tackling the roots of conflict and promoting sustainable development, the Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR) has entered into
posts.content:
Yemi Kosoko in Jos

In a bold move aimed at tackling the roots of conflict and promoting sustainable development, the Institute for Peace and Conflict Resolution (IPCR) has entered into a strategic partnership with Tomruk iHub Multiverse Limited to deploy technology-driven peace education programmes across Nigeria and ultimately, the African continent.

The partnership, formalised through the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), is expected to significantly expand access to peacebuilding knowledge by combining IPCR’s expertise in conflict prevention, management and resolution with Tomruk iHub’s digital infrastructure, technological innovation and extensive networks.

Under the agreement, the two organisations will drive the implementation of the Mass Peace Education Programme, designed to equip citizens, particularly young people, with practical skills for preventing violence, managing disputes and fostering peaceful coexistence in their communities.

Speaking at the signing ceremony, the Director-General of IPCR, Dr Joseph Ochogwu, described peace education as a vital national imperative that must be accessible to all citizens regardless of age, profession or educational background.

He stressed that sustainable peace can only be achieved when knowledge of conflict prevention and resolution is democratised and taken beyond traditional classrooms to reach every segment of society.

According to him, the partnership represents an innovative approach to broadening the reach of peace education through technology and strategic collaboration.

Also speaking, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Tomruk iHub Multiverse Limited, Mr Job Mwadkon Dachungyang, said Africa’s progress and prosperity depend largely on the capacity of its people and institutions to prevent and resolve conflicts effectively.

He noted that peace and conflict resolution skills are indispensable for national development, adding that no society can achieve lasting growth in an atmosphere of persistent conflict and instability.

Dachungyang reaffirmed the company’s commitment to leveraging technology to ensure that peace education reaches communities across Nigeria and beyond, regardless of location or social status.

The partnership will also explore specialised programmes focused on election violence prevention, non-violent engagement and conflict transformation, while extending peace education to both formal and informal learning environments.

Observers say the collaboration marks a significant milestone in the effort to institutionalise peace education and harness innovation as a tool for strengthening social cohesion and national unity.

For IPCR, the alliance reinforces its commitment to building peaceful, resilient communities and nurturing a culture of dialogue, tolerance and non-violence through education, innovation and strategic partnerships.

posts.title: Kano court orders destruction of over 400 bags of unsafe flour
posts.excerpt: A Kano court has directed the destruction of more than 400 bags of spoiled wheat flour seized by the Kano State Consumer Protection Council, KCPC, to stop the products from being sold to unsuspecting
posts.content:
A Kano court has directed the destruction of more than 400 bags of spoiled wheat flour seized by the Kano State Consumer Protection Council, KCPC, to stop the products from being sold to unsuspecting consumers.

The flour was confiscated after members of the public alerted the council to a large quantity of deteriorated products allegedly stored for sale despite being unsafe for consumption.

The council announced the court order in a statement issued on Wednesday by its Director of Public Enlightenment, Jamilu Mustapha Yakasai.

It said the legal action was taken to ensure that the seized flour would not find its way back into the market.

The Executive Secretary of the KCPC, Dr Ibrahim Garba Muhammad, said the council would continue to protect residents against contaminated, damaged, expired and substandard goods.

He explained that the agency was enforcing consumer protection laws, including taking legal action against traders who violate regulations.

Muhammad said, "The measures were necessary to safeguard public health and prevent residents from buying products that could put their lives at risk."

He urged traders to comply with the council's regulations, maintaining that its activities were not intended to intimidate or harass business owners but to promote lawful trading and protect consumers' rights.

The executive secretary also advised residents to examine the quality and safety of goods before purchasing them and report suspicious products or business practices to the council.

He commended Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf for supporting the agency, saying the assistance had strengthened its ability to carry out its responsibilities.

posts.title: Cross River court jails 38-year-old man for life over rape of 10-year-old girl
posts.excerpt: A Cross River State High Court has sentenced a 38-year-old man, Nsikak Friday Okon, to life imprisonment for raping a 10-year-old girl. Justice Blessing Egwu handed down the sentence in a judgment wel
posts.content:
A Cross River State High Court has sentenced a 38-year-old man, Nsikak Friday Okon, to life imprisonment for raping a 10-year-old girl.

Justice Blessing Egwu handed down the sentence in a judgment welcomed by child rights advocates as a significant step towards protecting children from sexual violence and abuse.

The Basic Rights Counsel Initiative, BRCI, which supported the survivor and her family throughout the legal proceedings, commended the court for the verdict.

The organisation also recognized the Cross River State Government, the Nigeria Police Force and the state Ministry of Justice for their roles in securing the conviction.

It specifically acknowledged the Attorney General of the state, Ededem Ani, the Director of Public Prosecutions, Okoi Ukam, and Joseph Apajung for their commitment to the prosecution of the case.

BRCI said supporting a child survivor of sexual assault went beyond securing a conviction, stressing the need to protect the victim's privacy and ensure access to appropriate care and support.

"Supporting survivors of sexual assault at that age goes beyond securing convictions. It means protecting their privacy, listening patiently to their needs and ensuring that they and their families get the support to heal and rebuild," the organisation said.

While describing the judgment as a step towards justice, BRCI urged stakeholders to ensure that survivors of sexual violence receive adequate protection, medical and psychosocial support.

The organisation called for sustained efforts to prevent sexual abuse and protect the rights, dignity and wellbeing of children.

posts.title: Stanbic IBTC Upgrades Enugu School with Classrooms, 20-Computer Laboratory
posts.excerpt: Funmi Ogundare Stanbic IBTC Holdings has renovated classrooms and administrative offices, installed a 20-computer laboratory and constructed modern sanitation facilities at New Haven Secondary School
posts.content:
Funmi Ogundare

Stanbic IBTC Holdings has renovated classrooms and administrative offices, installed a 20-computer laboratory and constructed modern sanitation facilities at New Haven Secondary School Enugu State, as part of efforts to improve access to quality education and digital learning across Nigeria.

The intervention, implemented under the financial institution’s Adopt-A-School initiative, also includes the provision of classroom furniture, a mini-library, a volleyball court and the planting of 60 trees within the school premises.

The facilities were recently handed over at a ceremony attended by representatives of the financial institution and the school community.

The upgraded classrooms, each designed to accommodate up to 40 students, are expected to improve teaching and learning outcomes for more than 500 students and staff.

The computer laboratory, equipped with 20 computers and dedicated workstations, is also expected to provide students with greater access to technology and practical digital skills needed for academic development and future career opportunities.

The Head, Commercial Banking South, Business and Commercial Banking, Stanbic IBTC Bank, Nnaemeka Obasi, who represented the Chief Executive of Stanbic IBTC Holdings, Chuma Nwokocha, reaffirmed its commitment to empowering future leaders through education.

“At Stanbic IBTC, we firmly believe that investing in education is investing in the future of our nation. By providing our students with the right tools and a conducive learning environment, we are nurturing the innovators, leaders and changemakers of tomorrow.

“This achievement represents another step forward in our commitment to transforming educational landscapes across Nigeria. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that all students have access to the resources and opportunities they need to thrive,” he said.

The initiative, he added, also seeks to promote students’ intellectual and physical development through the establishment of a mini-library to encourage reading culture and independent research.

Similarly, the construction of a volleyball court is expected to promote physical fitness, teamwork and students’ overall well-being, while the planting of 60 trees is aimed at encouraging environmental sustainability and awareness.

New Haven Secondary School is the 11th institution to benefit from Stanbic IBTC’s Adopt-A-School initiative, which focuses on improving educational infrastructure and creating conducive learning environments in schools across the country.

Nwokocha said the programme reflects its commitment to corporate social responsibility and supporting Nigeria’s educational development through targeted interventions designed to promote sustainable growth.

posts.title: E-DON Advances Digital Education With Indigenous QR Smart Board, 3D Technology
posts.excerpt: Kuni Tyessi in the Nigerian-led classroom revolution is underway as the College of Education (COE), Ikwo, Ebonyi State moves to adopt E-DON’s indigenous QR Interactive Smart Board and 3D Animation
posts.content:
Kuni Tyessi in the

Nigerian-led classroom revolution is underway as the College of Education (COE), Ikwo, Ebonyi State moves to adopt E-DON’s indigenous QR Interactive Smart Board and 3D Animation and Simulation Software, in a strategic shift from imported, chalk-and-talk teaching to interactive, technology-driven learning designed for Nigerian curricula.

The initiative is a major milestone in the drive to transform Africa’s educational landscape through local innovation, rather than dependence on imported solutions.

The Provost, Prof. Benedict Chukwuma Edigbo Mbam, speaking on behalf of the college, said the proposed adoption of E-DON’s homegrown technology marks a decisive step towards preparing teachers who can thrive in a digital world.

He said indigenous education technology innovator, E-DON, is advancing digital education in the country with its two flagship technologies designed to redefine how knowledge is delivered, understood and experienced in modern classrooms.

He noted that the QR Interactive Smart Board is designed to replace passive, chalk-and-talk teaching with interactive digital learning, making lessons more engaging, accessible and technology-driven.

He added that it will also serve as a complement to the 3D Animation and Simulation Software, which bridges the long-standing gap between theory and practice, and through 3D visualisation, animation and simulation, complex and abstract concepts in science, mathematics, geography, biology and technical subjects will become easier to understand, explore and remember.

“We cannot continue to train 21st-century teachers with 19th-century tools. Our responsibility is to prepare teachers who will walk into modern classrooms with confidence, with digital competence, and with the ability to make learning come alive for their own students.

“This technology will help our lecturers deliver better, our student-teachers learn better, and our college remain relevant, competitive and attractive to the next generation of learners. It is about quality, it is about relevance, and it is about the future,” Mbam said.

National Coordinator, The Electronic Education Initiative, E-DON, Dr. Idonuagbe Akogun, said indigenous innovation is the key to sustainable transformation.

He noted that E-DON has over the years demonstrated that Africa does not have to depend entirely on imported technology to solve its education challenges.

With creativity, research, collaboration and investment in indigenous technology, Nigeria can develop solutions that compete globally while addressing local realities.

“For too long, Africa has waited for imported solutions to solve African problems. E-DON is proof that we can design, engineer and build our own solutions, solutions that understand our curriculum, our culture, our classrooms, and our realities.

“The QR Interactive Smart Board and our 3D Animation and Simulation Software were not built in Silicon Valley. They were built in Nigeria, for Nigerian learners. When a student can see the human heart beating in 3D, or explore the solar system in simulation, learning stops being memorisation. It becomes experience,” Akogun said.

Meanwhile, E-DON remains committed to partnering with educational institutions to deliver technology-driven, practical and inclusive learning across Nigeria and Africa.

posts.content:
Gideon Arinze in Enugu

The governorship candidate of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) in Enugu State, Uche Nnaji, has linked the rising cases of criminality in the state to worsening economic hardship.

Nnaji, who spoke during a consultative visit to Enugu indigenes resident in Aba, Abia State Tuesday, alleged that economic activities in some rural markets had declined, with traders operating at night to avoid taxation.

In a statement issued by his media campaign team, the candidate said the situation reflected the economic difficulties confronting residents.

“So many people do not know what is happening. Markets in the villages have closed, with traders now coming out only at night to avoid paying taxes,” he said.

He also expressed concern over what he described as a resurgence of night-time robbery, alleging that criminals had resorted to breaking into homes to steal food and other basic valuables.

“Criminals have returned to operating between midnight and 4am, breaking into homes to steal food and other basic valuables. This reflects the severe level of hunger in the state and the economic hardship confronting our residents,” he added.

On his economic plans, Nnaji promised to establish three major manufacturing industries within his first two years in office if elected in 2027.

He said his proposed industrialisation drive would focus on processing local raw materials, particularly coal and iron ore deposits in areas including Awhum, Nachi and Nsukka.

He said the plan was aimed at creating employment opportunities and expanding economic activities in the state.

posts.title: THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…
posts.excerpt: sponsor : Tokunbo Wahab PEOPLE FIRST Hamzat’s PROMISE: Putting the Lagosian at the Centre of Governance This is an examination of the People First agenda and its 15 pledges on
posts.content:
sponsor : Tokunbo Wahab

PEOPLE FIRST

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Putting the Lagosian at the Centre of Governance

This is an examination of the People First agenda and its 15 pledges on healthcare, education, community safety and citizen services

Every political manifesto comes with an assortment of promises, but their importance is ultimately determined by how closely they address the needs of the people for whom government exists.

For a state such as Lagos, where rapid population growth continually stretches public infrastructure and services, the relationship between government and the ordinary resident is particularly important.

A parent concerned about the cost of medical treatment, a young graduate struggling to find employment, a trader confronted by harassment on the streets and a resident spending an entire day pursuing a government document may have different immediate concerns.

Yet, all four experiences raise a common question: how effectively does government respond to the needs of its citizens?

This is the question at the heart of the People First component of the Lagos PROMISE, the manifesto unveiled by the All Progressives Congress governorship candidate, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, ahead of the 2027 election.

Structured around four thematic areas and 15 distinct pledges, People First addresses healthcare, education and human capital, community safety, and the relationship between citizens and public institutions.

Of the 15 pledges, 11 are classified as firm commitments and four as aspirations. The distinction is significant because it separates proposed obligations from broader objectives whose achievement may depend on additional resources, external partnerships or conditions yet to be established.

Together, the pledges offer a framework for examining what people-centred governance would mean in practical terms.

Healthcare: From Building Hospitals to Improving Access

Healthcare occupies a central position in the People First agenda, with five pledges covering medical infrastructure, personnel, insurance, vulnerable populations and specialist treatment.

Among the proposed targets are a workforce of 9,000 doctors, two additional general hospitals, 120 flagship primary healthcare centres and 15 maternal and child centres by 2031. The manifesto also proposes expanding selected general hospitals, including those in Alimosho, Odan and Ikorodu.

These commitments address an enduring challenge of urban development: the tendency for population growth to outpace the availability of public services.

For Lagos, however, the issue extends beyond the number of healthcare buildings. A hospital is useful only to the extent that it has qualified personnel, functional equipment, essential medicines and the capacity to attend promptly to patients.

Consequently, the proposed expansion of healthcare facilities would need to proceed alongside effective staffing, maintenance and financing arrangements.

This is where the Pledge of Systems connects with the Pledge of the Healthcare Economy, which proposes extending Ilera Eko health insurance coverage to 30 per cent and strengthening the state’s medicine supply and healthcare financing systems.

The significance of insurance cannot be overstated. For many households, a serious illness is simultaneously a medical emergency and a financial crisis.

Wider insurance participation could help reduce the immediate pressure of paying for treatment, although the eventual benefit would depend on the services covered, participating facilities and affordability of premiums.

Another dimension is the Pledge of the Vulnerable, which sets targets for reducing malaria, maternal mortality and the burden of noncommunicable diseases, while expanding community mental healthcare across the five administrative divisions of Lagos.

Here, the distinction between inputs and outcomes becomes especially relevant.

The number of hospitals constructed can be counted. So can the number of doctors recruited. But the more consequential questions concern whether fewer mothers die during childbirth, whether more diseases are detected early and whether patients receive timely treatment.

These are the measures by which healthcare expansion would acquire meaning beyond physical infrastructure.

The fifth undertaking, the Pledge of Care on Lagos Soil, addresses specialist medical services and the ambition to reduce outbound medical tourism through facilities such as the Lagos Cancer Diagnosis Centre, Medipark and other specialist institutions.

Classified as an aspiration, it reflects a broader economic consideration: the possibility of retaining healthcare expenditure, professional expertise and medical investment within Lagos.

Its realisation would nevertheless require sustained investment in specialist personnel, equipment, quality assurance and the confidence of patients, who currently seek treatment elsewhere.

Education: Preparing the Lagos Mind for a Changing Economy

Education constitutes the second component of People First, with four pledges directed at learning outcomes, vocational training, tertiary education and access.

The Pledge of Foundations proposes strengthening the EKOEXCEL programme across public primary schools and extending its approach into secondary education.

This is particularly relevant because improvements at the primary level can be diminished if students enter secondary schools without adequate teaching support, continuity or a curriculum responsive to their needs.

But educational reform must also confront a question that has become increasingly important: what happens after students leave school?

Lagos operates in an economy where technology, logistics, construction, creative enterprise and other sectors are changing the nature of employment. Qualifications alone do not necessarily guarantee that young people possess the practical skills demanded by employers.

The manifesto therefore links its Pledge of Skills to technical and vocational education, including the proposed completion of Meiran Technical College, additional colleges in Ibeju-Lekki and Badagry, and an artificial intelligence workforce programme.

The policy implication is that education would be judged increasingly by its ability to connect learning with productive participation in the economy.

That connection, however, must be demonstrated rather than assumed.The number of students admitted into training programmes would tell only part of the story.

The more revealing measures would include completion rates, professional certification, apprenticeships, job placements and the extent to which employers recognise the skills acquired.

The Pledge of the Lagos Mind extends the reform agenda to universities, research institutions, teachers, lecturers and trainers.

Its inclusion acknowledges that expanding access to schooling without improving the quality of instruction would leave a major part of the education challenge unresolved.

Meanwhile, the Pledge of Equity seeks to improve educational opportunities for children irrespective of household income or personal circumstances, including reducing the number of out-of-school children.

Unlike some other undertakings in the manifesto, the proposed reduction is not accompanied by a precise numerical target.

That leaves room for a clearer implementation framework identifying the existing number of affected children, the annual reduction being pursued and the mechanisms for bringing them into and retaining them within the education system.

These questions matter because access, quality and employability are interconnected. A child excluded from education today becomes an adult with diminished economic opportunities tomorrow.

Community Safety: Beyond Conventional Crime Fighting

The third People First component deals with the experience of security at the neighbourhood level. Its four pledges cover local safety arrangements, crime prevention, complaints and protection for survivors of sexual violence.

The Pledge of the Neighbourhood proposes extending the reach of the Lagos Neighbourhood Safety Agency across the state’s 20 local government areas and 37 local council development areas.

The Pledge of Prevention seeks to strengthen community-based interventions involving schools, markets, motor parks and faith-based institutions.

Together, they reflect an approach in which public safety is not restricted to responding after crimes have been committed.

For residents, insecurity can manifest in relatively ordinary but persistent experiences: harassment in traffic, extortion at commercial locations, threats around markets or the absence of effective intervention when disputes escalate.

These experiences have economic as well as social consequences. They influence business operating costs, commuting patterns and public confidence in government.

The emphasis on prevention is therefore relevant, provided community participation translates into genuine intelligence-sharing, conflict resolution and accountable enforcement.

There is also an important institutional limitation. Policing remains principally a federal responsibility under Nigeria’s existing constitutional framework. The proposed state-level interventions would consequently require coordination with federal law enforcement authorities.

That makes clarity of responsibility essential. Residents should be able to distinguish between agencies responsible for receiving complaints, preventing disorder, investigating crimes and prosecuting offenders.

The Pledge of the Citizen Voice introduces specific response standards: acknowledgment of safety complaints within 24 hours, an initial response within seven days and resolution within 30 days.

Such targets provide a potentially useful basis for accountability. They would be more meaningful, especially if accompanied by publicly available data on complaints received, cases resolved and matters referred for further investigation.

The fourth undertaking, the Pledge of the Survivor, proposes expanding sexual-assault referral support across all five administrative divisions.

Beyond the availability of centres, effective protection would require confidential reporting, trained personnel, medical and psychological support, and reliable links to the justice system.

The essential issue is whether a person seeking protection can access it promptly and safely, regardless of location or financial circumstances.

Citizen Service: Making Government Easier to Reach

Perhaps the most immediately relatable aspect of People First is its final component: the way residents encounter government offices and public services. Two pledges define this agenda.

The Pledge of the Front Door proposes satellite government secretariats in Badagry, Ikorodu, Lagos Island and Epe, complementing the central secretariat at Alausa.

The underlying challenge is straightforward. A resident should not necessarily have to undertake a lengthy journey across Lagos merely to obtain information, submit an application or resolve an administrative problem.

Decentralising selected services could reduce transportation costs, time lost in transit and the concentration of administrative activities in Ikeja. Yet, the location of an office is only one part of accessibility.

The offices would need appropriately trained staff, functioning digital systems, clearly defined services and sufficient authority to resolve matters without repeatedly referring residents back to Alausa.

Otherwise, decentralisation could simply reproduce existing bureaucratic difficulties in additional locations.

The second undertaking, also described as the Pledge of the Citizen Voice, establishes standards for responding to public complaints.

Under the published manifesto, complaints are to be acknowledged within 24 hours, receive an initial response within seven days and, in routine cases, be resolved within 30 days. More complex matters are assigned a longer period in the accompanying implementation narrative.

These provisions provide clearer opportunities for measuring public-service performance.

For residents, the practical test would be whether applications are processed within advertised periods, complaints are assigned to identifiable officials and unresolved cases can be escalated without unnecessary difficulty.

The proposed integration of resident identification and government services could further simplify public administration, but it would also require dependable safeguards for personal information and effective alternatives for residents who lack smartphones or reliable internet access.

A government service is not genuinely accessible if the process excludes the people most in need of it.

2

…THE KOH MANIFESTO SERIES…

RENEWAL

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Rebuilding the Foundations of Greater Lagos

Beyond roads, bridges and rail lines, the Renewal agenda proposes a new relationship between infrastructure investment, economic productivity and the quality of everyday life.

Infrastructure has become one of the defining questions of governance in Lagos. Not necessarily because the state has failed to invest in it, but because the scale and speed of its growth continually place fresh demands on facilities that are already under pressure.

A road constructed today may struggle with traffic volumes in a few years. A drainage channel designed for an existing community may become inadequate as new estates emerge. Water infrastructure installed decades ago must contend with changing population patterns, while electricity supply remains an expensive uncertainty for households and businesses.

This is the context in which Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, has situated the second pillar of his 2027 governorship manifesto, The Lagos PROMISE.

Known simply as Renewal, the agenda contains 12 pledges distributed across four areas: roads and transport infrastructure, electricity, water supply, and waste management and flood resilience.

Taken together, they raise a larger question about the future of Lagos: can infrastructure development move beyond the construction of new facilities to the creation of systems that are dependable, properly maintained and capable of supporting a growing megacity?

Roads and Bridges: The Importance of What Already Exists

The first three pledges, contained under Building Greater Lagos, address roads and bridges, traffic junctions and rail development.

The Pledge of Roads and Bridges proposes rehabilitating the state road network and restoring bridges to publicly defined standards.

Its significance lies partly in its recognition that maintenance should be treated as an essential component of infrastructure policy rather than an occasional intervention.

Lagos has invested in major roads, bridges and transport corridors under successive administrations. Yet, the experience of commuters demonstrates that the condition of smaller connecting roads can be just as consequential as the existence of major highways.

A journey shortened by a new expressway may still be frustrated by badly maintained feeder roads, damaged intersections or inadequate drainage.

The challenge, therefore, is not only how many kilometres of road are constructed, but how effectively the entire network operates. The Pledge of the Junction addresses a particularly familiar Lagos experience: traffic congestion at critical intersections.

Hamzat proposes a continuous junction-improvement programme beginning with ten identified priority locations, alongside the restoration of traffic signals across the state within the first year.

The importance of this proposal is that congestion is not always caused by an absolute shortage of roads. Inefficient junction designs, poor signal coordination, roadside trading, indiscriminate parking and weak enforcement can reduce the capacity of existing infrastructure.

A comparatively modest junction intervention can sometimes improve traffic flow without the financial and environmental implications of constructing an entirely new road.

But the effectiveness of such measures must be tested through average travel times, traffic speeds and commuter experience, rather than the mere commissioning of redesigned intersections.

Rail Development and the Question of Connectivity

The Pledge of Rail commits to completing the Blue Line extension to Okokomaiko and linking the Red and Blue lines at the National Theatre, Iganmu. This is an important distinction in the development of Lagos mass transit.

A rail line does not derive its full value simply from the distance it covers. Its wider significance emerges when passengers can transfer conveniently between services and complete journeys without unnecessary delays or additional costs.

The proposed connection between the two lines would therefore represent more than a construction milestone. It would address a fundamental problem in urban mobility: fragmentation.

For Lagos to realise the potential of its rail investments, stations must connect effectively with buses, ferries, taxis and other transport services.

The manifesto also discusses the Fourth Mainland Bridge and major federal transport corridors. These, however, involve approvals, financing and institutional arrangements beyond the direct authority of the state government.

The distinction matters because a state administration may control the maintenance of its roads while having a more limited ability to determine the completion of federally controlled or jointly financed infrastructure.

Electricity: The Search for Reliable Power

The second component of Renewal, named IMOLE, addresses electricity through three pledges. Its most ambitious target is the Pledge of Light, an aspiration to increase grid electricity reaching households from approximately 1,000 megawatts to 3,500 megawatts by 2031.

The manifesto acknowledges that Lagos requires substantially more electricity than it currently receives. The proposed increase is therefore a contribution towards addressing an identified deficit, rather than a guarantee that the state’s entire electricity requirement would be met.

The distinction between an aspiration and a firm commitment is particularly relevant here.

Electricity delivery depends on generation, transmission, distribution, financing and regulation.

Although the Electricity Act 2023 and subsequent state legislation have expanded the opportunities for subnational electricity markets, the state cannot independently guarantee every part of the supply chain.

The Pledge of the Market proposes strengthening the Lagos State Electricity Regulatory Commission and establishing a phased state electricity market in partnership with the major distribution companies.

The Pledge of the Renewable Pathway complements this with embedded generation for industrial parks and wider deployment of renewable energy and mini-grid solutions.

For businesses, reliable electricity is not merely a matter of convenience. It affects production costs, competitiveness, employment and the price eventually paid by consumers.

A workshop that spends substantial sums on diesel or petrol generation must recover those costs somehow. A hospital without dependable electricity faces operational risks. A waterworks without reliable power cannot guarantee continuous supply.

Electricity reform therefore connects directly with the other components of Renewal.

Its success would need to be measured not only in megawatts added but in actual hours of supply, affordability, metering, network reliability and reductions in dependence on private generators.

Water: The Infrastructure That Enters Every Home

Water supply forms the third component of Renewal. The manifesto proposes, through the Pledge of the Tap, expanding treatment capacity using Adiyan Phase II and rehabilitating existing waterworks, with the stated objective of providing six million additional residents with clean water every day.

The Pledge of the Regulator seeks to strengthen oversight of water quality, tariffs and service delivery, while the Pledge of the Water Tariff addresses affordability through a proposed Water and Sanitation financing arrangement.

These pledges address a critical problem that does not always receive the political attention accorded to roads or bridges. In many Lagos communities, households depend on privately drilled boreholes, commercial water vendors and other alternatives to reliable public supply.

The consequences extend beyond convenience. Families incur recurring costs in obtaining water, while inadequately regulated sources can create serious public-health concerns.

Completing Adiyan Phase II would represent an important infrastructure milestone. Yet, expanded treatment capacity would not automatically guarantee access unless transmission mains, distribution networks and household connections function effectively.

This is why the proposed rehabilitation of existing waterworks must be considered alongside the expansion programme. There is also a delicate policy balance between financial sustainability and affordability.

Water infrastructure requires substantial capital and recurring maintenance expenditure. At the same time, pricing arrangements must protect households whose incomes cannot support high service charges.

A credible implementation programme would therefore need to show how expanded supply, tariff regulation and support for vulnerable households would operate together.

Waste Management and Flood Resilience

The final three Renewal pledges fall under the ILE MIMO programme, covering waste collection, drainage and environmental resilience.

Through the Pledge of Collection, Dr. Hamzat proposes achieving 95 per cent waste-collection coverage by 2030, supported by community collection arrangements, four transfer stations, a material recovery facility and a waste-to-energy facility.

The manifesto also proposes incorporating informal waste pickers into a more organised system through training, equipment and improved working conditions.

The policy significance extends beyond environmental cleanliness. Waste management is increasingly a question of public health, employment, resource recovery and climate resilience.

Improperly disposed refuse can obstruct drainage channels, contribute to flooding and expose communities to disease.

The Pledge of Clear Drains consequently proposes sustaining primary and secondary drainage maintenance and the Emergency Flood Abatement Gang.

The Pledge of Resilience addresses coastal and low-lying communities through climate adaptation and early-warning arrangements.

These undertakings are interconnected. A drainage channel cannot function effectively when it is filled with refuse, just as improved waste collection cannot eliminate flood risks arising from inadequate drainage capacity, unregulated development or coastal exposure.

For a low-lying coastal state, flood management must increasingly be treated as continuous risk reduction rather than an emergency response whenever heavy rainfall occurs.

The proposed 95 per cent waste-collection target offers a measurable benchmark. But its implementation would have to address collection frequency, equitable coverage, the treatment of collected waste and the long-term financial viability of the system.

OPPORTUNITY

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Turning Lagos’ Economic Strength into Jobs and Prosperity

With 23 pledges spanning enterprise, food security, maritime development, culture, technology and public finance, the Opportunity agenda examines how the state’s economic advantages could translate into broader participation and household prosperity.

Lagos has never suffered from a shortage of economic ambition. From its sprawling markets and industrial estates to its financial institutions, technology companies and creative enterprises, the state remains a principal centre of commercial activity in Nigeria.

But behind the impressive concentration of business activities lies a more complicated reality.

The prosperity generated by a major commercial centre does not automatically translate into prosperity for everyone who lives and works within it. A growing economy can coexist with unemployment, inadequate infrastructure, expensive credit and millions of small businesses struggling to survive.

It is this contradiction that gives the Opportunity component of Dr. Hamzat’s manifesto its underlying significance.

Containing 23 pledges across six thematic areas, Opportunity is the largest component of The Lagos PROMISE. It addresses enterprise and investment, food security, the maritime economy, culture and tourism, technology, and the management of public finances.

Its central proposition is that Lagos must not simply accommodate economic activity. It must develop the institutions, infrastructure and policies that enable more residents and businesses to participate productively in that economy.

Enterprise: From Informality to Economic Opportunity

The first four pledges concern enterprise development, industrial expansion, investment and opportunities for women. The Pledge of Investment sets an aspiration to increase annual investment from approximately N1 trillion towards N5 trillion by 2031 through a proposed Invest in Lagos platform and investment pipeline.

Alongside it, the Pledge of the Million seeks to expand the number of formal micro, small and medium enterprises from about 120,000 towards one million, supported by the N10 billion LASMECO financing programme.

The targets are ambitious, but their significance lies in the economic problem they attempt to confront. Many Lagos residents conduct legitimate commercial activities outside the formal business system.

They trade, manufacture, provide services and employ workers, yet often lack access to affordable credit, insurance, structured markets and opportunities to participate in government procurement.

Formalisation could create pathways to these benefits, provided the process does not become another source of administrative charges and regulatory burdens.

The manifesto proposes simplifying business registration, reducing obstacles to permits and addressing multiple levies affecting enterprises.

These are important considerations because the willingness of informal businesses to enter the formal economy depends substantially on whether they can see practical benefits from doing so.

The Pledge of the Parks proposes delivering four industrial parks at Epe, Badagry, Ikorodu and Ojo under the state’s 2025–2030 industrial policy. Industrial parks could support manufacturing by concentrating infrastructure, logistics, power and essential services in designated locations.

However, the effectiveness of such parks would depend on occupancy, transport connections, utility reliability, financing and the extent to which they support sustainable production rather than becoming underused industrial estates.

The fourth undertaking, the Pledge of the Women-Led Floor, reserves at least 50 per cent of beneficiaries in state enterprise programmes for women-led businesses.

Its implementation would raise important questions about eligibility, transparent beneficiary selection and whether participation translates into improved business survival, profitability and access to new markets.

Food Security: The Economics of the Lagos Plate

Food constitutes the second component of Opportunity. This is especially relevant to Lagos because the state combines a large consumer population with relatively limited agricultural land.

The Pledge of the Plate seeks to increase food self-sufficiency from a stated baseline of approximately five per cent through local production, aquaculture and stronger integration with agricultural production elsewhere in Nigeria.

It is classified as an aspiration, reflecting the reality that Lagos cannot independently produce everything its population consumes.

The Pledge of the Cold Chain proposes operationalising the 420-hectare Lagos Food Logistics Hub and expanding refrigerated storage and transportation facilities to reduce post-harvest losses.

The Pledge of Supply commits to sustaining the Produce-for-Lagos offtake programme and the Lagos Bulk Food Company, while expanding mid-level fresh-food hubs across the 20 local government areas.

The economic logic is relatively straightforward. Food prices are influenced not only by the quantity produced on farms but also by the costs of transportation, storage, distribution and wastage.

When produce deteriorates between farms and markets, the losses are eventually reflected in higher prices. When supply chains are inefficient, consumers pay for those inefficiencies.

Improved logistics and storage could reduce some of these costs. But a food-security strategy must also distinguish between greater availability and affordability. Food can be present in markets while remaining beyond the purchasing power of low-income households.

Consequently, the most meaningful measures would include price stability, reduced spoilage, better market access and the proportion of household income spent on food.

The manifesto also proposes a Food Intelligence System to monitor prices, availability and supply risks. Such a system could help anticipate disruptions, although its usefulness would depend on reliable data and the government’s ability to respond to emerging shortages.

The Blue Economy: Turning Water into Productive Assets

Lagos possesses geographical advantages that extend beyond conventional land-based commerce. Its coastline, lagoon, ports, creeks and inland waterways support substantial opportunities in transport, logistics, fisheries, tourism and maritime services.

Yet, much of the economic potential associated with water remains insufficiently integrated into the state’s wider development strategy.

The Opportunity agenda addresses this through three pledges. The Pledge of the Waterways proposes expanding the Lagos State Waterways Authority ferry network and the OMI EKO partnership.

The Pledge of the Seafarer Development Pathway seeks to train, certify and create international placement opportunities for Lagos residents in maritime occupations.

The Pledge of Value, classified as an aspiration, proposes retaining more shipping, maritime services, aquaculture and fisheries-related economic value within Lagos. These commitments go beyond passenger ferry operations.

A functioning maritime economy requires ship maintenance, logistics services, navigation, insurance, port support, fisheries processing, training and other professional activities.

It also requires a deliberate connection between transport infrastructure and the communities surrounding it.

A ferry terminal, for example, can function as more than a passenger facility. When properly planned, it can support retail businesses, hospitality services and other economic activities.

The manifesto’s proposal to examine five potential mini-ports in Badagry, Ikorodu, Epe, Lekki and Lagos Central is relevant in this regard.

But maritime development also involves significant federal regulatory responsibilities. Port administration, maritime safety and international shipping cannot be governed independently by the state. This makes federal-state cooperation indispensable.

The potential economic benefits must also be balanced against environmental protection, the livelihoods of existing fishing communities and the cost of establishing viable infrastructure.

Culture and Tourism: The Economy Beyond Entertainment

Three pledges address culture, heritage and tourism. The Pledge of the Stage proposes a Lagos Creative Economy financing window and supporting infrastructure for film, music and fashion.

The Pledge of Heritage seeks to preserve cultural assets and establish a structured cultural calendar involving major traditions such as Eyo and Gelede.

The Pledge of Tourism proposes strengthening the Lagos Tourism Board and developing cultural resources into commercial visitor experiences. The importance of these proposals lies in the recognition that culture is simultaneously an expression of identity and a source of employment.

Lagos already has an established creative ecosystem, particularly in film, music and fashion. Yet, the economic benefits extend far beyond performers and producers.

The creative economy supports technicians, transport operators, hospitality businesses, event organisers, designers, marketers and numerous other service providers.

Developing this economy would require more than festivals and promotional campaigns. It would involve suitable venues, professional training, reliable electricity, safe transport, intellectual property protection and financing arrangements that enable smaller operators to grow.

Heritage preservation also demands sensitivity. Commercial development should not undermine the cultural ownership, historical significance or traditional institutions associated with the festivals and sites being promoted.

The wider test would be whether culture-driven investment produces sustainable employment and revenue while protecting the identity of the communities involved.

Technology: Producing Innovation Rather Than Merely Consuming It

The technology component, known as IMO, contains seven pledges and is one of the most detailed parts of the Opportunity agenda. Its Pledge of Training proposes equipping one million young people with technology-related skills over four years and connecting training to employment opportunities.

The Pledge of Connectivity addresses broadband access, fibre infrastructure and digital connectivity for schools, hospitals, businesses and underserved communities.

The manifesto also seeks to expand the state’s fibre network from about 2,700 kilometres to 6,800 kilometres. These proposals recognise that digital participation increasingly influences access to education, employment, finance and public services.

However, training numbers should not be confused with employment outcomes. The real test would be how many participants complete their programmes, gain recognised qualifications and secure sustainable work or establish viable businesses.

The Pledge of the Builder expresses an aspiration to make Lagos a leading location for establishing technology companies through research financing and government procurement opportunities.

The Pledge of Sovereignty proposes a cybersecurity centre and a framework for protecting public data. The Pledge of the First Buyer seeks to allocate 10 per cent of relevant government procurement towards innovations developed in Lagos.

This last undertaking is economically significant. For many start-ups, the difficulty is not merely developing a product but obtaining an initial customer willing to adopt it.

Government procurement can help bridge that gap, provided public contracts remain competitive, transparent and based on demonstrable value.

The Pledge of the Innovation Legal Entity proposes developing the Lagos State Science, Research and Innovation Council into a more substantial innovation agency, supported by legislation, matching grants and mechanisms for commercialising research.

Finally, the Pledge of What We Invent proposes a Lagos Patent Bank to support the protection and commercialisation of intellectual property created within the state. Such an institution would require careful coordination with Nigeria’s existing intellectual property laws and international obligations.

The broader objective is to create stronger links between research institutions, entrepreneurs, investors and markets, so that locally developed technologies have pathways to commercial success.

Public Finance: The Treasury Behind the Promises

The final three Opportunity pledges concern public finance. The Pledge of Revenue proposes expanding internally generated revenue through a broader tax base rather than higher tax rates.

The Pledge of Restraint commits to borrowing within sustainable debt-service limits and publishing the use of borrowed funds.

The Pledge of One Treasury proposes keeping financing instruments within a consolidated treasury framework, subject to audit and public scrutiny. These commitments are central to the credibility of the wider manifesto.

Infrastructure, healthcare, education, housing and economic development all require substantial resources. Without adequate financing, even carefully designed programmes can become difficult to deliver. Yet, raising more revenue does not necessarily require imposing higher rates on existing taxpayers.

Reducing leakages, improving compliance, simplifying payment systems and widening legitimate participation in the tax system can potentially improve collections.

Borrowing also has a legitimate place in financing long-term infrastructure, but repayment obligations must remain consistent with the state’s capacity to service debt.

Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat (KOH

The proposed treasury framework would therefore need to provide information on project costs, borrowing terms, debt-service commitments and independently verified expenditure.

The Difference Between Growth and Prosperity

The 23 pledges under Opportunity bring together several economic questions that are often discussed separately. How does Lagos attract investment while improving conditions for small businesses? How can food logistics help reduce costs?

How does maritime infrastructure generate employment? How can technology training produce actual jobs? And how can government finance all these undertakings without imposing unsustainable obligations? The common thread is productivity.

Economic expansion becomes more meaningful when businesses operate at lower costs, workers earn sustainable incomes, producers gain access to markets and public resources are deployed efficiently.

But these outcomes cannot be established by investment announcements or programme enrolment figures alone. They require evidence of enterprise survival, employment creation, rising productivity, improved incomes and greater participation across different communities.

Opportunity represents more than a programme for attracting investment. Its eventual public significance would depend on whether the wealth associated with Lagos’ commercial strength becomes more widely reflected in the economic circumstances of the people who sustain it.

MACHINERY OF GOVERNMENT

Hamzat’s PROMISE: Re-engineering Government for Efficiency & Accountability

The Machinery of Government agenda addresses a fundamental question: can Lagos improve the institutions responsible for delivering public services, administering justice and accounting for public resources?

Government is often judged by what it builds, commissions or distributes. Roads, hospitals, schools and housing estates are visible expressions of public investment. They attract attention and provide convenient measures of administrative performance.

Yet, beneath these visible achievements lies another dimension of governance that may be even more consequential: the capacity of public institutions to function efficiently.

A well-equipped hospital cannot deliver its intended benefits if procurement procedures fail to provide medicines. A newly constructed school will struggle without qualified teachers. A court building cannot guarantee justice if cases remain unresolved for years.

Ultimately, the effectiveness of public investment depends substantially on the machinery that manages it.

This is the argument underlying the fourth pillar of Dr. Hamzat’s governorship manifesto, The Lagos PROMISE.

Known as Machinery of Government, the pillar contains nine pledges organised around public service reform, intergovernmental cooperation, justice administration, digital government and public accountability.

Unlike the more visible infrastructure and economic components, these proposals are concerned with the institutional arrangements that determine how government works.

Reforming the Public Service

The first undertaking, the Pledge of the Public Service, proposes a merit-based, performance-driven and technology-enabled civil service. For Lagos, the issue goes beyond the professional development of government employees.

Public administration increasingly requires specialised knowledge in engineering, finance, information technology, urban planning, data management, environmental protection and numerous other fields.

The quality of public-service recruitment, training, promotion and performance management therefore influences the quality of government decisions. A merit-based system would seek to connect advancement more closely with competence and demonstrable performance.

However, such reforms must also address employee welfare, institutional stability and the protection of professional decision-making from undue political interference.

The purpose should not simply be to introduce new evaluation procedures, but to ensure that public servants have the skills, resources and motivation to carry out their responsibilities effectively.

The Lagos Compact: Connecting Institutions

The Pledge of the Compact proposes operationalising a six-component governance framework across the manifesto. This is complemented by two pledges bearing the title Pledge of the Council.

One addresses cooperation with the Lagos State Council of Obas and Chiefs, while the other proposes establishing a Lagos State Economic Council through which the governor and selected executive officials would engage local government and local council development area chairmen.

The proposal recognises that development is shaped by institutions operating at different levels.

A state ministry may construct a major drainage channel, but local authorities and community institutions remain important to preventing blockages and maintaining the surrounding environment.

Similarly, public health, markets, waste collection and neighbourhood planning require coordination between state and local institutions.

The proposed Economic Council could provide a forum for identifying local priorities, monitoring delivery and resolving intergovernmental difficulties.

Its effectiveness would depend on the authority of its decisions, the transparency of its proceedings and whether it produces measurable improvements rather than becoming another administrative gathering.

The emphasis on traditional institutions also reflects their continuing relevance to community engagement and local dispute resolution.

However, consultation must remain consistent with established democratic structures and the constitutional responsibilities of elected authorities.

Justice: Bringing the Courts Closer to the People

Three pledges address the justice system. The Pledge of the Nearer Court proposes increasing the civil monetary jurisdiction of magistrates’ courts from N10 million to N50 million, expanding court facilities and improving support for magistrates.

The Pledge of Legal Access seeks to extend legal assistance through the Office of the Public Defender and the Citizens’ Mediation Bureau. The Pledge of Forensic Justice proposes strengthening forensic facilities, including DNA analysis, sexual-assault investigations and cyber-forensic capabilities.

Together, these proposals address important obstacles to the administration of justice: cost, distance, delay and investigative limitations. For many residents and small businesses, pursuing a legal remedy can be expensive and time-consuming.

Expanding the jurisdiction of magistrates’ courts, subject to the necessary legal changes, could enable more civil disputes to be handled closer to the communities where they arise.

Likewise, effective mediation can help resolve suitable disputes without the expense and delays associated with prolonged litigation.

But improved access must not undermine the quality of justice.

Increasing court jurisdiction would need to be accompanied by adequate judicial personnel, improved facilities, case-management systems and procedural safeguards.

Forensic improvements could also strengthen the quality of investigations, particularly in sexual violence and technologically sophisticated offences.

Their practical value would depend on scientific standards, trained specialists, reliable evidence handling and the capacity of investigators and prosecutors to make appropriate use of the facilities.

Crucially, the manifesto acknowledges judicial independence and administrative support must not become interference in the exercise of judicial powers.

Digital Government: Beyond Putting Forms Online

The Pledge of the Benchmark proposes measuring Lagos’ digital government against leading international standards and publishing performance dashboards. The broader chapter discusses integrated digital identity, improved service delivery, data management and cybersecurity.

The importance of this proposal lies in recognising that digital government means more than replacing paper forms with online applications.

A genuinely integrated digital service should reduce duplication, simplify transactions and enable government institutions to share relevant information through lawful and secure arrangements.

Consider the experience of a resident seeking several government approvals. Under a fragmented system, the individual may repeatedly submit the same documents to different agencies, visit multiple offices and make separate inquiries about the status of applications.

An integrated system could reduce these difficulties by establishing common service standards and improving communication between institutions.

But digitalisation can also create new problems. Residents without reliable internet access, digital literacy or suitable devices may encounter difficulties if physical service channels disappear.

Data protection is equally important. The concentration of personal information within government systems requires secure access arrangements, clear legal safeguards and mechanisms for addressing misuse.

Therefore, the proposed digital benchmarks are intended to examine not only the number of services moved online but also processing times, system reliability, user satisfaction and accessibility.

The Hamzat Compact: Making Performance Verifiable

The ninth undertaking, the Pledge of the Charter, proposes publishing a service charter for every ministry, department and agency, specifying service standards and response times. It belongs to the broader Hamzat Compact, which the manifesto presents as its accountability framework.

The underlying idea is that citizens should be able to establish what government has promised to deliver, who is responsible and whether the undertaking has been fulfilled. This would represent an important departure from performance reporting that relies mainly on general statements of achievement.

For example, an agency responsible for processing permits could be required to state the expected completion period and publish data showing how consistently it meets that standard.

A public hospital could report waiting times and service availability. An infrastructure agency could publish project milestones, expenditure and completion records.

But meaningful accountability requires more than government-generated reports. Published information should be sufficiently detailed for independent examination, and the methodology used to measure performance should be clear.

The manifesto’s broader commitment to public scorecards and citizens’ monitoring would therefore require credible baselines, accessible records and channels through which residents can challenge inaccurate claims.
